meta.title: Occult Upper-Airway Foreign Body Mimicking Anaphylaxis
meta.summary: 55M brought by EMS from a restaurant with sudden-onset dyspnoea and audible wheeze. Every monitor number is normal at the door. Prior neck cancer treated with chemoradiotherapy, a food allergy without an auto-injector, hypertension and dyslipidaemia set a trap: the hidden truth is a piece of steak lodged immediately above the vocal cords. The core history must be in hand by 2:00 or he starts to fail; repeated anaphylaxis treatment without airway reassessment ends in hypoxic PEA.
meta.author: Prepared from learner-described simulation case

objectives.overall_goal: Recognise a time-critical partial upper-airway foreign body that initially mimics anaphylaxis or bronchospasm, and escalate from focused history and exam to definitive airway management before hypoxic arrest.
medical: Rapidly obtain focused history and EMS collateral in a dyspnoeic patient.

Integrate sudden onset while eating, short-sentence speech, audible wheeze, absence of rash/urticaria/oropharyngeal oedema, and failure to respond to anaphylaxis treatment into the differential for upper-airway obstruction.
Use appropriate first-line epinephrine for suspected anaphylaxis in a patient with a pulse (IM, not the 1 mg IV arrest dose).
Recognise when to perform direct/video laryngoscopic airway assessment and foreign-body extraction.
Perform hypoxic PEA resuscitation with high-quality CPR, airway management and ACLS epinephrine when deterioration occurs.
nursing: Recognise early clinical deterioration despite initially normal monitor values.
Provide prompt cues when the learner repeatedly treats presumed anaphylaxis without reassessing the airway.
Prepare airway, suction, Magill forceps, RSI medications and resuscitation equipment as requested.
crm: Maintain a shared mental model and closed-loop communication during a rapidly evolving airway emergency.
Reassess the diagnosis when treatment response is absent.
Assign roles early for airway, medications, monitoring and CPR preparation.
epas: Resuscitation of the critically ill patient

patient.name: JM
allergies: Food allergy (exact trigger not specified); no epinephrine auto-injector
past_medical_history: Neck cancer treated with radiotherapy and chemotherapy, now in remission
social_history: Was out for dinner at a restaurant when this started
patient.persona: 55-year-old man, frightened and working hard to breathe. Speaks only in short sentences of three to six words and pauses for breath between them. Sitting bolt upright on the stretcher; will not lie flat. You do not know what is wrong — it came on all at once while you were eating dinner. If asked what you think it is, you wonder aloud whether it is your food allergy. You have never had anything like this before. If asked: a 'sort of neck cancer' a few years ago treated with chemo and radiotherapy, now in remission; a food allergy but no EpiPen with you; high blood pressure and cholesterol; amlodipine 5 mg and atorvastatin 20 mg once a day. Do not describe any sensation in the throat unless directly asked, and then only say it feels tight and hard to get air in. Never name a foreign body or say something is stuck.

presentation.opening_vignette: We have a 55-year-old man brought in by ambulance for difficulty breathing and wheezing. He's on the stretcher. His initial monitor values and ECG are normal. EMS are still here if you want the handover.
triage_note: Brought by EMS from a restaurant for sudden-onset difficulty breathing and audible wheezing.
Visibly distressed but haemodynamically stable and oxygenating normally on arrival.

history.label: EMS handover
history.content: He was at a restaurant when he suddenly started having trouble breathing and wheezing. Staff called us. He's stayed awake the whole way in and can answer, but only in short sentences. No trauma. Nothing infectious going on before this that anyone knows of. Sats were fine on scene so we didn't give anything.

history.label: Onset of symptoms (patient)
history.content: It came on all at once. I was eating — dinner, steak — and suddenly I couldn't get a proper breath. It's been like this since. Never had anything like it.

history.label: Past history and allergies (patient)
history.content: I had a sort of neck cancer a few years back — chemo and radiotherapy. They say it's in remission. I've got a food allergy — I don't carry an EpiPen. Blood pressure and cholesterol are the other things.

history.label: Medications (patient)
history.content: Amlodipine, five milligrams, and atorvastatin, twenty. Both once a day. Nothing else.

findings: Visible respiratory distress; speaks in short sentences
Sitting upright, will not lie flat
exam.note: Distress is out of proportion to the monitor: every number on the screen is normal.

findings: Wheeze on auscultation, loudest centrally; no focal crackles
Increased work of breathing with accessory-muscle use
exam.note: The wheeze is loudest over the upper airway rather than the chest — a monophonic, transmitted quality.

findings: Oropharynx clear on routine inspection; no visible foreign body, no pooling of secretions
Post-radiotherapy skin changes over the anterior neck; no mass, no trauma
exam.note: Routine mouth and oropharyngeal inspection is unrevealing. Nothing below the tongue base can be seen without a laryngoscope.
The counter-clue: a patient this distressed from anaphylaxis would be expected to show skin signs.

findings: Normal S1 and S2, regular rhythm, no murmur
Moving all four limbs, speech content normal though clipped by breathlessness

actors.voice: Frightened, breathless; short clipped sentences with pauses to breathe.
actors.persona: See patient.persona. Answers only what is asked and does not know what is wrong. Becomes drowsy and monosyllabic if the team delays; speaks normally again only once the airway is relieved.
Paramedic handing over at the bedside. Knows only what happened at the scene and in the truck.
script: He was at a restaurant when he suddenly started having trouble breathing and wheezing. Staff called us. He has stayed awake and can answer briefly. No trauma.

actors.persona: Bedside nurse. Executes orders, reports vitals and results, and prompts the team when it is stuck.
script: Asks which specific tests are wanted when the resident says 'labs' or 'bloodwork'.
Confirms the epinephrine dose before drawing it up, and pushes back on the 1 mg IV arrest dose while the patient has a pulse.
If an awake scope is attempted without any analgesia or airway plan: 'He's not tolerating this — do you want something for analgesia, or a different airway plan?'
If anaphylaxis is treated repeatedly without reassessment: 'He's not getting better — could something be obstructing the airway?'

actors.persona: Airway assistant. Prepares the video laryngoscope, suction, ETT, BVM and Magill forceps on request and performs the video laryngoscopy when asked. Puts the view up on the GlideScope screen and lets the resident read it — never describes or names what is seen.
script: Prepares scope, suction, tubes, bougie and Magill forceps when asked.
Performs video laryngoscopy on request and announces only that the view is up on the screen.

actors.persona: On-call otolaryngologist reached by phone. Wants to know what the airway looks like before offering a plan.
script: Before a laryngoscopic view exists: asks whether anyone has looked at the cords, and says to scope him and call back with what is seen.
Once a supraglottic food bolus has been seen: Magill forceps under video laryngoscopy if it can be reached; otherwise induce, intubate and push it into a main bronchus for bronchoscopic retrieval.
After intubation: will arrange rigid bronchoscopy in theatre or the unit.

actors.persona: Intensivist on the phone. Accepts only a patient whose airway is secured.
script: If called before the airway is secured: 'We're flat out up here. Diagnose and treat him first — call me when he's tubed.'
Once intubated: accepts, asks for ventilator settings and a post-intubation gas.

actors.persona: Anaesthetist reached in theatre. Cannot come down for several minutes and says so; never arrives and offers no management.
script: 'We're mid-case. Someone can come down in a few minutes. Until then you'll have to manage the airway yourself.'

investigations.name: CBC
investigations.interpretation: Unremarkable. Nothing here explains the respiratory distress.

investigations.name: CHEM 10
investigations.result: Na 139, K 4.1, Cl 103, HCO3 24, urea 5.3, creatinine 88, glucose 6.2, Ca 2.34, Mg 0.82, phosphate 1.12.

investigations.name: Venous blood gas
investigations.result: VBG: pH 7.38, pCO2 43 mmHg, HCO3 25 mmol/L, base excess 0.

result_by_state.deteriorating: VBG: pH 7.24, pCO2 58 mmHg, HCO3 25 mmol/L.
result_by_state.pea_arrest: VBG: pH 7.08, pCO2 70 mmHg, HCO3 20 mmol/L.
result_by_state.death: VBG: pH 7.08, pCO2 70 mmHg, HCO3 20 mmol/L.

investigations.interpretation: Normal while he is compensating. In the deteriorating state the gas shows hypercapnic respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation past a partial obstruction; peri-arrest it is a severe mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis.

investigations.name: Lactate
investigations.interpretation: Normal at baseline; rises with hypoxia and hypoperfusion as he deteriorates, markedly elevated peri-arrest.

investigations.name: Liver function tests
investigations.result: AST 24, ALT 27, ALP 82, total bilirubin 11, albumin 42.

investigations.name: High-sensitivity troponin
investigations.interpretation: Negative. A repeat without a new cardiac indication stays non-diagnostic.

investigations.name: 12-lead ECG
investigations.result: 12-lead ECG recorded; the tracing is up on the monitor for you to read.
investigations.interpretation: Normal sinus rhythm at about 92/min, normal axis and intervals, no acute ischaemic change. The heart is not the problem.

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Portable chest film is on the screen for you to review.
investigations.interpretation: No focal infiltrate, oedema, pneumothorax or radio-opaque airway foreign body. A soft-tissue food bolus above the cords is not visible on a chest film.
investigations.visual_dx: normal chest, no acute cardiopulmonary process

investigations.name: Point-of-care ultrasound (cardiac and lung)
investigations.result: No pericardial effusion; grossly preserved LV systolic function; no RV strain. Bilateral lung sliding present; no B-lines, no pleural effusion.
investigations.interpretation: Nothing on ultrasound explains the respiratory distress — it argues against tamponade, PE, pneumothorax and pulmonary oedema.

investigations.name: Video laryngoscopy
investigations.result: GlideScope, suction and Magill forceps are at the bedside; ready to look when you have an airway plan.

result_by_state.fb_visualized: View obtained at the glottic inlet; the image is on the GlideScope screen.
result_by_state.vl_aborted: He's gagging and fighting the blade — no view. Attempt abandoned.
result_by_state.pea_arrest: View obtained; the image is on the GlideScope screen.
result_by_state.intubated_displaced: Tube is through the cords; the image is on the GlideScope screen.
result_by_state.recovery: Cords clear, no residual material; the image is on the GlideScope screen.

investigations.interpretation: Food bolus (steak) impacted immediately above the vocal cords, partially obstructing the glottic inlet — the diagnosis. Removable with Magill forceps under the scope.

states.name: Baseline — sudden dyspnoea and wheeze
states.patient_status: Awake, alert and oriented. Visible respiratory distress with an audible wheeze; speaks in short sentences. Every monitor value is normal.
expected_actions: Rapid ABC assessment
EMS handover and focused history: sudden onset while eating, allergy, past history, medications
Focused exam including skin and airway
Name each investigation individually

modifiers.description: Ninety seconds in: he is tiring, the rate creeps up and the saturation slips.

cues.text: EMS are still here at the foot of the bed if you want the story from them.

transitions.description: Core history obtained in time: how it started (handover or onset) and the background (past history/allergy or medications).
transitions.patient_effect: The story is in hand: sudden onset while eating, an allergy with no auto-injector, a radiated neck. He is still perfusing and oxygenating.

transitions.description: Treats as anaphylaxis and gives epinephrine.
transitions.patient_effect: Epinephrine in. He is still wheezy and working hard; nothing much changes.

transitions.description: Suspects a mechanical upper-airway obstruction at the door and moves to look at the airway.
transitions.patient_effect: The team pivots to the airway. He is anxious and will not lie flat.

transitions.description: Two minutes pass without the core history in hand; he begins to fail while still perfusing.
transitions.patient_effect: He's getting sleepy on us and the sats are drifting down. Pressure's dropping — he still has a pulse.

states.facilitator_notes: Normal monitor values are intentionally misleading; the clinical distress is the signal. The 2:00 history gate is the first checkpoint.

states.name: Checkpoint — history in hand, synthesis
states.patient_status: Awake, distressed, wheezy, speaking in short sentences. Still perfusing and oxygenating. Any tests sent in the first two minutes are now back.
expected_actions: Focused exam: skin (no urticaria), mouth and neck, chest
Synthesise: sudden onset while eating, no skin signs, transmitted upper-airway wheeze
Decide between treating anaphylaxis and reassessing the airway for mechanical obstruction

modifiers.description: He is tiring: rate up, saturation drifting.

cues.text: He's still wheezy and working hard, and there's no rash anywhere. What's your read?

transitions.description: Treats as anaphylaxis and gives epinephrine.
transitions.patient_effect: Epinephrine in. He is still wheezy and working hard; nothing much changes.

transitions.description: Reconsiders mechanical obstruction and moves to the airway.
transitions.patient_effect: The team pivots to the airway. He is anxious and will not lie flat.

transitions.description: Two more minutes without a decision; he begins to fail while still perfusing.
transitions.patient_effect: He's getting sleepy on us and the sats are drifting down. Pressure's dropping — he still has a pulse.

states.facilitator_notes: Second checkpoint: synthesis after the focused exam. The learner should reconsider mechanical obstruction before repeated medication cycles or a broad workup.

states.name: Deteriorating but perfusing
states.patient_status: Somnolent, reduced speech, worsening respiratory effort. Hypoxic and hypotensive but still has a pulse.
expected_actions: Immediate airway-focused reassessment
Oxygen and bag-mask support
Decisive airway action: look at the cords now

modifiers.description: Forty seconds in: saturation falling fast, heart rate climbing — the monitor is alarming.

cues.text: Sats are seventy-eight and falling. Do you want the scope in his mouth now?

transitions.description: Decisive airway action: laryngoscopy or intubation. He is obtunded enough to tolerate the blade.
transitions.patient_effect: He's not fighting it. Blade's in — the view's up on the screen.

transitions.description: Reconsiders mechanical obstruction and calls for the airway kit.
transitions.patient_effect: The airway kit is open at the bedside. He is drowsy and no longer fighting.

transitions.description: Treats as anaphylaxis and gives epinephrine.
transitions.patient_effect: Epinephrine in. Pressure comes up a little; he is still hypoxic and drowsy.

transitions.description: Continued delay past the rescue window: hypoxic PEA arrest.
transitions.patient_effect: He's gone unresponsive — no pulse. There's an organised rhythm on the monitor. He's in PEA.

states.facilitator_notes: Not yet arrest. This is the rescue window: the learner should recognise impending complete obstruction and hypoxic collapse.

states.name: Anaphylaxis pathway — first dose given
states.patient_status: Working diagnosis anaphylaxis; one dose of epinephrine given. Still wheezy and distressed, no meaningful improvement. No rash, no lip or tongue swelling.
expected_actions: Reassess after the dose: no durable response
Note the absent skin signs and oral oedema
Reconsider mechanical obstruction and look at the airway

modifiers.description: No reassessment a minute after the dose: he is tiring, saturation drifting down.

transitions.description: Reassesses the airway after the failed dose and reconsiders mechanical obstruction.
transitions.patient_effect: The team pivots to the airway. He is anxious and will not lie flat.

transitions.description: Gives a second dose of epinephrine.
transitions.patient_effect: Second dose in. Heart rate up, tremulous — the wheeze and the work of breathing are exactly the same.

transitions.description: Waits on the drug; he begins to fail while still perfusing.
transitions.patient_effect: He's getting sleepy on us and the sats are drifting down. Pressure's dropping — he still has a pulse.

states.facilitator_notes: After the first IM dose there is no meaningful improvement. A second dose is defensible if anaphylaxis is still suspected, but the lack of response should prompt airway reconsideration. Never present 1 mg IV as routine anaphylaxis treatment in a patient with a pulse.

states.name: Anaphylaxis pathway — second dose, no response
states.patient_status: Two doses of epinephrine given with no response. Persistent, worsening obstruction; tachycardic and tremulous from the drug, getting drowsy.
expected_actions: Stop and reassess the diagnosis
Examine and visualise the airway

modifiers.description: Forty-five seconds on: saturation and pressure falling.

cues.text: He's not getting better. Could something be obstructing the airway?

transitions.description: Finally reassesses the airway and reconsiders mechanical obstruction.
transitions.patient_effect: The team pivots to the airway. He is drowsy and no longer resisting.

transitions.description: A third epinephrine trial without airway reassessment: hypoxic PEA arrest.
transitions.patient_effect: Third dose in — and he's gone. Unresponsive, no pulse, organised rhythm on the monitor. PEA.

transitions.description: Waits on the drug; he begins to fail while still perfusing.
transitions.patient_effect: He's getting sleepy on us and the sats are drifting down. Pressure's dropping — he still has a pulse.

states.facilitator_notes: Reproduces the original sim logic: more than two sequential epinephrine trials without addressing the airway leads to PEA.

states.name: Mechanical obstruction suspected — airway reassessment
states.patient_status: Awake, distressed, cannot comfortably lie supine. Obstruction persists. Airway kit, suction and Magill forceps at the bedside.
expected_actions: Prepare suction, Magill forceps and airway backup
Make a deliberate airway plan: analgesia/sedation or RSI, backup, roles
Controlled video-laryngoscopic assessment

modifiers.description: A minute of preparation without looking: he is tiring.

cues.text: Scope, suction and the Magills are ready. How do you want to do this — awake, or with something on board?

transitions.description: A planned, controlled laryngoscopy: analgesia, sedation, topical anaesthesia or an explicit airway plan before the blade goes in.
transitions.patient_effect: He settles with it on board. Blade's in — the view's up on the screen.

transitions.description: Proceeds straight to RSI; induction and laryngoscopy give the view.
transitions.patient_effect: Induced and paralysed. Blade's in — the view's up on the screen.

transitions.description: Awake laryngoscopy with no analgesia, sedation or airway plan: he resists and the attempt is abandoned.
transitions.patient_effect: He's gagging and fighting the blade — he won't tolerate this. No view. Do you want something for analgesia, or a different airway plan?

transitions.description: Attempts modified abdominal thrusts or back blows on the stretcher.
transitions.patient_effect: Two rounds of thrusts on the stretcher. Nothing comes up. He is more distressed than before.

transitions.description: Two minutes of preparation without a look; he begins to fail while still perfusing.
transitions.patient_effect: He's getting sleepy on us and the sats are drifting down. Pressure's dropping — he still has a pulse.

states.facilitator_notes: Sedation in a precarious airway is a deliberate airway plan, not an automatic fentanyl requirement. The planned attempt is listed first so it wins whenever the plan was voiced; the bare attempt fires only when it was not.

states.name: Abdominal thrusts — nothing expelled
states.patient_status: Thrusts attempted on the stretcher; nothing expelled. Still obstructed, more distressed, tiring.
expected_actions: Move to airway visualisation with a deliberate plan

cues.text: Nothing's shifted. The scope is right here if you want to look.

transitions.description: A planned, controlled laryngoscopy after the failed manoeuvre.
transitions.patient_effect: He settles with it on board. Blade's in — the view's up on the screen.

transitions.description: Proceeds to RSI; induction and laryngoscopy give the view.
transitions.patient_effect: Induced and paralysed. Blade's in — the view's up on the screen.

transitions.description: Awake laryngoscopy with no plan: he resists and the attempt is abandoned.
transitions.patient_effect: He's gagging and fighting the blade — he won't tolerate this. No view. Do you want something for analgesia, or a different airway plan?

transitions.description: A minute passes after the failed manoeuvre; he begins to fail while still perfusing.
transitions.patient_effect: He's getting sleepy on us and the sats are drifting down. Pressure's dropping — he still has a pulse.

states.facilitator_notes: Default case branch: the manoeuvre fails because the object sits above the cords and is not expelled. Proceed to airway visualisation.

states.name: Awake laryngoscopy aborted
states.patient_status: Attempt abandoned: he gagged and fought the blade. No view. More distressed, saturation slipping.
expected_actions: Analgesia or sedation as a deliberate plan, or move to RSI
Re-attempt controlled laryngoscopy with suction and forceps ready

modifiers.description: Thirty seconds after the abort: saturation slips further.

cues.text: He's not tolerating this. Do you want something for analgesia, or a different airway plan?
cues.when: no new plan after the abort

transitions.description: Re-attempts with analgesia, sedation or an explicit airway plan on board.
transitions.patient_effect: He settles with it on board. Blade's in — the view's up on the screen.

transitions.description: Moves to RSI; induction and laryngoscopy give the view.
transitions.patient_effect: Induced and paralysed. Blade's in — the view's up on the screen.

transitions.description: No new plan; he begins to fail while still perfusing.
transitions.patient_effect: He's getting sleepy on us and the sats are drifting down. Pressure's dropping — he still has a pulse.

states.facilitator_notes: Cue the need for a deliberate airway plan — analgesia/sedation, backup, suction and forceps — rather than treating fentanyl as a universally required step.

states.name: View obtained at the cords
states.patient_status: Blade in, view on the GlideScope screen. Sedated or induced; tolerating the scope. Saturation is holding in the low nineties and will not hold for long.
expected_actions: Read the view on the screen
Remove the object with Magill forceps under the scope, or
Intubate and displace it distally for later bronchoscopic retrieval

modifiers.description: Thirty seconds with the blade in and nothing done: saturation falling.

cues.text: Blade's in and I've got the view — want it up on the screen? What's the plan?

transitions.description: Removes the object with Magill forceps under video laryngoscopy.
transitions.patient_effect: Out in one piece. Immediate improvement — he takes a full breath, the wheeze is gone, sats climbing. He can speak in full sentences.

transitions.description: Intubates; the tube pushes the object into a main bronchus and ventilation is restored.
transitions.patient_effect: Tube's through. Something went distal with it — good chest rise on the right, quieter on the left. Sats coming up on the ventilator.

transitions.description: View obtained and nothing done for ninety seconds: hypoxic PEA arrest.
transitions.patient_effect: He's gone unresponsive — no pulse. There's an organised rhythm on the monitor. He's in PEA.

states.facilitator_notes: The reveal is the picture on the screen (the video laryngoscopy card), not a spoken finding. Nobody in the room names what is seen. Extraction is the preferred endpoint; intubation with distal displacement is the salvage branch.

states.name: Recovery — airway relieved
states.patient_status: Immediate improvement after extraction. Breathing easily, wheeze resolved, speaking in full sentences. Enormously relieved.
states.facilitator_notes: Preferred successful endpoint. Proceed to debrief.

states.name: Intubated — ventilating
states.patient_status: Intubated and sedated, ventilating. Saturation and haemodynamics recovered. Air entry is asymmetric: the object has gone down one main bronchus.
expected_actions: Confirm tube position
Post-intubation sedation and ventilator settings
Arrange ICU and ENT/bronchoscopy for definitive retrieval

cues.text: He's ventilating well on the right, quiet on the left. Who do you want to call for the bronchoscopy?

transitions.description: States the disposition: ICU admission with bronchoscopic retrieval arranged.
transitions.patient_effect: Accepted to ICU, ventilated, with bronchoscopy arranged for retrieval.

transitions.description: Time passes on the ventilator; the team completes the disposition.
transitions.patient_effect: Accepted to ICU, ventilated, with bronchoscopy arranged for retrieval.

states.facilitator_notes: Alternate salvage branch. Ventilation improves but definitive bronchoscopic retrieval is still required.

states.name: Disposition — ICU and bronchoscopy
states.patient_status: Intubated, sedated and accepted to ICU with bronchoscopic retrieval arranged.

states.name: PEA arrest (hypoxic)
states.patient_status: Unresponsive and pulseless. Organised electrical activity without a pulse. Hypoxia is the presumed cause.
expected_actions: High-quality CPR
Oxygenate and ventilate; attach pads
ACLS epinephrine 1 mg IV every 3-5 minutes
Secure the airway and address the obstruction

cues.text: No pulse — he's in PEA. Do you want me to start compressions?

transitions.description: ROSC after CPR, a secured airway and two doses of arrest-dose epinephrine, in any order.
transitions.patient_effect: Pulse check — there's a pulse. Sinus tach on the monitor, pressure's coming up. ROSC.

transitions.description: No resuscitation step within sixty seconds of the arrest.
transitions.patient_effect: Asystole on the monitor. No pulse, no respiratory effort, pupils fixed. He's gone.

states.facilitator_notes: PEA endpoint per the design: high-quality CPR plus airway management plus two ACLS epinephrine doses gives ROSC. If the airway is visualised during intubation the facilitator may show the object and allow removal or passage as part of the resuscitation.

states.name: ROSC
states.patient_status: Post-arrest perfusing rhythm with a secured airway. Ventilated, sedated.
expected_actions: Post-ROSC care: confirm the airway, ventilator settings, post-arrest gas
Treat the cause: definitive foreign-body plan
Arrange ICU, ENT and bronchoscopy

cues.text: He's holding a pressure. Where's he going, and who's taking that thing out of his airway?

transitions.description: States the disposition: ICU with a definitive foreign-body plan.
transitions.patient_effect: Accepted to ICU post-arrest, with bronchoscopy arranged.

transitions.description: Time passes post-ROSC; the team completes the disposition.
transitions.patient_effect: Accepted to ICU post-arrest, with bronchoscopy arranged.

states.facilitator_notes: End the scenario after the team states the disposition and a definitive foreign-body plan. Debrief anchoring, reassessment after failed therapy and airway planning.

states.name: Disposition — ICU post-arrest
states.patient_status: Intubated, sedated and accepted to ICU post-arrest with a definitive foreign-body plan.

states.name: Death — unresuscitated arrest
states.patient_status: Asystole. No pulse, no respiratory effort. The patient has died.
states.facilitator_notes: End state: the arrest was not resuscitated. Proceed to debrief.

medication_rubric.label: Used the IM anaphylaxis dose of epinephrine
medication_rubric.note: Anaphylaxis with a pulse is treated with 0.5 mg (0.3-0.5 mg) of 1 mg/mL epinephrine IM — never the 1 mg IV arrest dose.

workup_rubric.label: Examined the skin for urticaria
workup_rubric.note: No hives, flushing or angio-oedema in a patient this distressed argues strongly against anaphylaxis.

workup_rubric.label: Examined the mouth and neck
workup_rubric.note: No lip or tongue swelling; a routine look is unrevealing, which is itself the prompt to look lower with a scope.

workup_rubric.label: Assessed breathing at the bedside
workup_rubric.note: The wheeze is monophonic and loudest over the upper airway — transmitted, not bronchospasm.

workup_rubric.label: Visualised the airway with the video laryngoscope
workup_rubric.note: The object sits above the cords and is only seen with direct or video laryngoscopy — the diagnostic reveal.

debrief.summary: A partial upper-airway obstruction from a food bolus lodged above the vocal cords, presenting as sudden dyspnoea and wheeze after a restaurant meal in a man with a food allergy and a radiated neck. The monitor is normal at the door and the food exposure, allergy history and wheeze pull the team toward anaphylaxis. The counter-clues are abrupt onset while eating, no hives or rash, no oropharyngeal swelling, a persistent focal airway problem, and no meaningful response to appropriate IM epinephrine. The object is seen only with video laryngoscopy and comes out with Magill forceps; intubation with distal displacement is the salvage; delay or repeated treatment without airway reassessment ends in hypoxic PEA.
teaching_points: Diagnostic anchoring: food exposure + allergy history + wheeze does not equal anaphylaxis. Reassess when the treatment response is absent.
The first two minutes are high-yield: sudden onset while eating, short-sentence speech, the allergy and the past history should all be in hand by 2:00.
Absent skin signs (urticaria, flushing, angio-oedema) and absent oropharyngeal swelling in a distressed patient argue against anaphylaxis.
Epinephrine for anaphylaxis with a pulse is 0.3-0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL IM. The 1 mg IV dose is for cardiac arrest only.
A routine mouth exam does not see the supraglottis. When an upper-airway obstruction is on the differential, look with a laryngoscope.
Awake instrumentation of a precarious airway needs a deliberate plan — analgesia or sedation, topical anaesthesia, suction, Magill forceps, backup — not an automatic drug.
Extraction under video laryngoscopy with Magill forceps is the preferred endpoint; if it cannot be reached, intubate and displace it distally for bronchoscopic retrieval.
Hypoxic PEA: high-quality CPR, oxygenate and ventilate, secure the airway, arrest-dose epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and fix the cause.
common_errors: Anchoring on anaphylaxis and giving repeated epinephrine without reassessing the airway.
Ordering the 1 mg IV arrest dose for a patient who has a pulse.
Treating normal monitor values as reassurance while the patient is visibly failing.
Attempting awake laryngoscopy with no analgesia, sedation or airway plan.
Sending a broad bloodwork panel instead of looking at the airway.

discussion.question: What features distinguish upper-airway foreign-body obstruction from anaphylaxis?
discussion.answer: Abrupt onset while eating, a monophonic transmitted wheeze or stridor loudest over the neck, no urticaria/flushing/angio-oedema, no lip or tongue swelling, and no response to IM epinephrine. Anaphylaxis usually has skin or mucosal involvement plus a second system, and improves with epinephrine.

discussion.question: How should epinephrine be dosed for anaphylaxis versus cardiac arrest?
discussion.answer: Anaphylaxis with a pulse: 0.3-0.5 mg of the 1 mg/mL (1:1000) preparation IM into the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed. Cardiac arrest: 1 mg of the 0.1 mg/mL (1:10,000) preparation IV/IO every 3-5 minutes. Giving 1 mg IV to a perfusing patient risks malignant arrhythmia and hypertensive crisis.

discussion.question: What is a deliberate plan for laryngoscopy in an awake, distressed patient with a suspected supraglottic foreign body?
discussion.answer: Preoxygenate; suction, Magill forceps, bougie and a surgical airway kit open; a second operator; topical anaesthesia or a dissociative dose of ketamine (or judicious fentanyl) to allow a look while preserving respiratory drive; or, if the obstruction is critical, RSI with a plan to push the object distally if it cannot be retrieved.

discussion.question: What are the priorities in hypoxic PEA?
discussion.answer: High-quality compressions with minimal interruption, oxygenation and ventilation, a secured airway, epinephrine 1 mg every 3-5 minutes, and treating the reversible cause — here, the obstruction. Pushing the object past the cords to ventilate is acceptable if it cannot be removed.

references: AHA/ILCOR adult foreign-body airway obstruction and PEA guidance.
